title: UF 18 cacao (NSIC Cc 08): Characteristics
metaDescription: UF 18 cacao is a cacao variety from Puentespina Farm. See its days to harvest, yield, pest ratings, traits and where it grows best.
excerpt: UF 18 is a registered cacao variety, also sold or known as NSIC Cc 08. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council (NSIC) in 3110 as NSIC 2008 Cc 08. Puentespina Farm bred it.

heroImage.alt: Young fruit trees planted in straight rows on cleared red soil, the kind of farm where UF 18 cacao is grown

blocks.text: If you came here looking for NSIC Cc 08, this is the same cacao. The facts below come from the NSIC registry kept by the Bureau of Plant Industry, with notes from its seller and farm sources. Compare it with the others in our [cacao variety finder](/crop-varieties/cacao), or see [every crop variety](/crop-varieties) we list. For the crop itself, read our guide: [Land preparation for tree crops](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation).

blocks.text: When does it bear, and how much?

A registered tree variety is described from its mother tree, not from trial plots. It first bore pods about 24 months after planting. A grafted or marcotted tree bears years sooner than one grown from seed, and its yield climbs as the tree grows.

Is it resistant to pests and diseases?

blocks.caption: Reactions in the registry trials, rated under natural field conditions
rows: Took some damage but held up

blocks.text: It was weak against coffee/pod borer, so scout for it from the early weeks.

The pests and diseases that hit cacao fields most often: [black pod of cacao](/diseases/cacao-black-pod), [cacao pod borer](/pests/cacao-pod-borer), [mealybug](/pests/mealybug). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Harvest:** First flowers about 24 months, pods about 29 months after planting.
**Fruit:** Red pods with white striped ridges turning orange yellow, about 41 beans per pod, 100 dry beans about 166 g.
Tolerant to pod rot, moderately resistant to dieback, susceptible to cacao pod borer.

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: highest yield figure in the NSIC cacao list, registered by a private farm. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant UF 18 cacao

Plant grafted clones, and mix two or three, because many cacao clones need another clone nearby to set pods. Pick by pod yield and bean size. A registered tree variety is a selection from one proven mother tree, and only grafted, budded or marcotted plants carry its traits. A seedling grown from its seed can turn out quite different. So buy from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, and ask which mother tree the scions came from. Before planting, get the field ready with our guide: [Pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).

items: Buy grafted or budded plants from an accredited nursery, with the variety name on the tag.
Ask your municipal agriculturist or nearby farmers how it did in your area last season.
Plant a few trees first if the variety is new to your area, before you fill the whole farm.
Write down the planting day, inputs and harvest, so you can compare varieties on your own ground. anee.io keeps these records for you.

items.q: Is NSIC Cc 08 the same as UF 18?
items.a: Yes. NSIC Cc 08 is another name for UF 18, registered as NSIC 2008 Cc 08. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: Where can I buy planting material of UF 18?
items.a: Buy grafted, budded or marcotted trees from a nursery accredited by the Bureau of Plant Industry, so you get the true variety. Ask your provincial agriculture office for the nearest one.
